subject: money
topic: How real estate ownership dictates the health outcomes of the working class
angle: While homeownership is linked to better health for some populations, evidence suggests these benefits may not apply to racial/ethnic minorities and may depend on house values.
title: The Geography of Health

hooks.text: Does owning a home actually make you healthier?
You assume homeownership is a health guarantee. The evidence says otherwise.
You are living in the shadow of historic redlining.
A set of keys on a kitchen counter.
Homeownership and health are not universally linked.

reveal.headline: Homeownership does not guarantee better health for everyone.
reveal.body: The health benefits of owning a home depend on your race, ethnicity, and the value of the property. Evidence is mixed or contested.

explain.headline: The link is inconsistent.
explain.body: Research shows homeownership is linked to health for non-Latino Whites, but not for many other groups. Benefits may also depend on house values. Most studies are observational and cannot prove causation.

matters.headline: Systemic history shapes your body.
matters.body: Historic redlining is linked to modern-day health outcomes across a person's lifespan. That may be why your neighborhood's history affects your physical well-being today.

example.headline: A walk past a boarded-up building.
example.body: You walk down a street where the houses have been neglected for decades. You feel the weight of the history in the cracked pavement.

question.headline: Who decided where your health begins?

stat.label: evidence for improved adult health from housing affordability interventions

claims.text: There is little evidence that owning a home has beneficial effects on children's cognitive achievement, behavior problems, and health.
claims.quote: We find little evidence of beneficial homeownership effects and suggest that previous analyses may have mistaken selection differences for the effect of homeownership itself.

claims.text: Homeownership is linked to health outcomes for non-Latino Whites, but this association is not statistically significant for racial/ethnic minorities.
claims.quote: Although homeownership was a robust, independent predictor for each health outcome in the non-Latino White population, the association disappeared in statistical significance for racial/ethnic minorities.

claims.text: The health-promoting effects of homeownership may be contingent upon house values.
claims.quote: Findings are consistent with the thesis that health-promoting effects of homeownership may be contingent upon house values.

claims.text: Historic redlining is linked to modern-day health outcomes across the lifespan.
claims.quote: This review demonstrates the persistent effect of historic redlining on individuals' health.

claims.text: Interventions that promote housing affordability and stability were associated with improved adult health outcomes, but the evidence is mixed and mostly low-certainty.
claims.quote: This systematic review found mixed and mostly low-certainty evidence that interventions that promote housing affordability and stability were associated with improved adult health outcomes.

verdict: The evidence does not support a universal link between homeownership and improved health, as the effects are inconsistent across different demographics and socioeconomic conditions.
caveat: Most studies are observational and cannot establish whether homeownership causes better health or if healthier people are simply more likely to own homes.
caption:
The link between homeownership and health is not universal. 

Research shows that while some groups see health benefits from owning a home, these effects are inconsistent across different demographics and socioeconomic conditions. Most studies are observational and cannot establish if homeownership causes better health or if healthier people are simply more likely to own homes.
